project.name: bookwise
project.description: Bookwise is an evidence-first, private book summarization platform combining a NestJS API, a Next.js web app, and a private Python processing service that uses Vertex AI Gemini for summaries and embeddings on GCP.

nodes.name: Dockerfile
nodes.summary: Three-stage Docker build for the Next.js web app: installs pnpm workspace dependencies, builds apps/web with NEXT_PUBLIC API and Auth0 settings baked in as build args, and runs a non-root production image on port 3000 via the root-env launcher script.
nodes.languageNotes: NEXT_PUBLIC_* values are passed as ARG and promoted to ENV in the builder stage because Next.js inlines them into the client bundle at build time, not at runtime.

nodes.name: dependencies
nodes.summary: Base stage on node:24-bookworm-slim that enables corepack and installs the pnpm workspace with a frozen lockfile using only root, web, and api package manifests.

nodes.name: builder

nodes.name: runtime
nodes.summary: Production stage that copies node_modules and the built web app, exposes port 3000, runs as UID 1000, and starts Next.js through scripts/run-next-with-root-env.mjs.

nodes.name: Dockerfile
nodes.summary: Three-stage Docker build for the NestJS API: installs pnpm workspace dependencies, compiles services/api, and runs the compiled dist/main.js as a non-root container exposing port 3001.
nodes.languageNotes: Multi-stage build keeps only node_modules and compiled output in the runtime image, separated from the build toolchain.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to see what Bookwise is: a private book summarization platform where every summary is backed by evidence. It covers the three runtime pieces (a NestJS API, a Next.js web app and a Python processing worker), local setup with Docker Compose and migrations, how summaries are published, Vertex AI configuration and GKE deployment. Keep these three services in mind, because the rest of the tour follows a book as it moves through them.

tour.title: Service Architecture Decision
tour.description: This architecture spec explains the main split in the system. The NestJS backend owns the PostgreSQL `app` schema, and the Python processing service owns the `data` schema. The spec also sets the permissions, the event flow and the clean-architecture layout that both services follow. That ownership boundary explains why the API and the worker never call each other directly and instead coordinate through database tables.

tour.title: Foundational Database Schema
tour.description: The first migration puts the spec's schema split into SQL. It creates app-side users, books, book_objects and the processing_commands queue, plus data-side processing_runs, processing_events and generated_summaries. It also enables pgvector for embeddings. The processing_commands table is the hand-off point between the API and the worker, and the steps that follow keep returning to it.
tour.languageLesson: SQL migrations are applied in order and recorded in a ledger table (here public.schema_migrations with checksums). Each migration should run exactly once, and a recorded migration should never be edited afterwards; schema changes go into a new numbered file instead.

tour.title: API Bootstrap and Wiring
tour.description: main.ts is the API entry point. It loads the environment, starts NestJS on Fastify with CORS and global validation, and listens on the configured port. app.module.ts has the highest fan-out in the codebase: it is the composition root that connects the Postgres pool, the OIDC verifier, the repositories, object storage (MinIO or GCS) and the use cases to the HTTP controllers. Read it as the API's table of contents.
tour.languageLesson: NestJS uses dependency injection with factory providers. A module declares how to build each dependency (often from environment variables) and binds it to a token. Classes then ask for the token instead of creating concrete implementations themselves, which keeps domain code free of infrastructure details.

tour.title: Domain Ports and Identity
tour.description: book.ts and auth-principal.ts are the two most-imported API files. They define the domain vocabulary: upload formats and size limits, the library and summary types, domain errors, and the repository, storage and token-verifier 'ports' that the wiring from Step 4 fills in. The authenticated-principal guard and the OIDC verifier use these ports to check Auth0 bearer tokens against a cached JWKS, so every request is tied to an owner.
tour.languageLesson: In TypeScript you can't inject an interface at runtime, because types are erased when the code compiles. Projects therefore pair each port interface with a Symbol or string DI token, so NestJS can resolve the right implementation while the domain layer depends only on the abstract type.

tour.title: Upload and Queue Commands
tour.description: This is the first half of a book's journey. BooksController issues an upload ticket and then finalizes the upload. FinalizeUploadUseCase checks that the object actually exists in storage, moves the book to the queued state, and has the processing-command repository insert paired ingest and regenerate-summary commands into app.processing_commands. Because these inserts are idempotent, a finalize request that is retried does not queue the work twice.

tour.title: Worker Runtime and Command Claiming
tour.description: The Python worker takes over from here. main.py just calls run_worker, and bootstrap.py is the worker's composition root, mirroring app.module.ts from Step 4: it wires repositories, storage, model providers and use cases, then polls for commands. commands.py defines the command, run and event records and the allowed run-state transitions. The claim use case and command_repository take queued commands with leases and advisory locks, so two workers never process the same book.
tour.languageLesson: Python's `python -m package.module` runs a module as a program. Keeping main.py tiny and putting the wiring in bootstrap.py follows the composition-root pattern: only one place knows about concrete implementations, and the rest of the code receives them as constructor arguments.

tour.title: Ingestion and Format Parsers
tour.description: When an ingest_book command is claimed, the ingest use case downloads the original file, sends it to the PDF, EPUB or DOCX parser, and normalizes the result into source spans and structure nodes. source.py, a central domain module, gives every span a deterministic UUIDv5 ID and a SHA-256 hash. Those stable IDs are what let a later summary cite an exact location in the book.
tour.languageLesson: Frozen dataclasses (`@dataclass(frozen=True)`) give Python immutable value objects. Combined with content hashing and UUIDv5 (name-based, deterministic UUIDs), they make ingestion reproducible: parsing the same book twice gives the same IDs.

tour.title: Evidence-First Summary Generation
tour.description: This step is the 'evidence-first' part of the project. generate_summary.py loads the normalized source from Step 8, asks the model provider for evidence and then a summary, validates both, builds embeddings, and records which stage failed if something goes wrong. generation.py holds the rules for chunking, validating output and hashing, and model_provider.py switches between Vertex AI Gemini and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint based on environment variables.

tour.title: Citations and Summary Projections
tour.description: The data schema enforces the evidence guarantees at the database level as well. Migration 003 adds source documents, spans and structure nodes with provenance triggers and row-level security. Migration 004 adds evidence, citations and pgvector embedding records with immutability triggers. Migration 006 exposes only the current, accepted summary through views, which keeps the read side in the next step simple.
tour.languageLesson: PostgreSQL row-level security (RLS) attaches policies to a table so each query only sees rows that pass a condition, such as owner_id = current_owner_id(). Triggers can also reject UPDATEs to enforce immutability. Both rules live in the database, so they apply to any client that connects, not just code that remembers to check.

tour.title: Reading Published Summaries
tour.description: Back in the API, the read path closes the loop. SummaryController serves `GET /v1/books/:bookId/summary`, and GetBookSummaryUseCase delegates to the read repository. That repository queries the projection views from Step 10 for the owner's library, the processing status and the published summary with citation locations. The API only ever reads the data schema here; it never writes to it.

tour.title: Web App and API Client
tour.description: The Next.js home page only shows the library once Auth0 has signed the user in. Underneath it, bookwise-api.ts attaches bearer tokens and validates every API response against the Zod schemas in library-types.ts, so the API contract from Steps 6 and 11 is checked again in the browser. The library screen lists books, polls the status of books still in progress, and opens the upload dialog.
tour.languageLesson: Zod schemas do two jobs in TypeScript: `z.infer<typeof Schema>` produces the static type, and `Schema.parse()` validates untrusted JSON when the code runs. This keeps compile-time types and runtime checks from drifting apart at the network boundary.

tour.title: Book Detail and Citations
tour.description: The dynamic `/books/[bookId]` route renders BookDetailScreen, where the user sees the end result. The screen polls the book's processing status every five seconds while work is in progress, then displays the published, evidence-backed summary with its citations. This is where the stable span IDs from Step 8 and the citation tables from Step 10 become visible to the user.
tour.languageLesson: In the Next.js App Router, a folder named `[bookId]` defines a dynamic route segment. The page component receives the matched value through `params`, so a single file serves every book's detail page.

tour.title: Local Development Stack
tour.description: To run everything yourself, docker-compose.yml starts pgvector-enabled PostgreSQL 17, Redis and MinIO; MinIO stands in for cloud object storage, with a one-time job that creates the bucket. start-local.ps1 checks prerequisites, starts that stack, waits for Postgres, runs the migration runner from Step 3, and opens terminals for the API, web app and worker, the three services traced through this tour.
tour.languageLesson: docker-compose health checks plus `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` make a service wait until another is actually ready, not just started. One-shot init containers like minio-init handle setup tasks such as creating buckets.

tour.title: CI/CD and GKE Deployment
tour.description: The reusable Verify workflow lints and builds the web app, API and worker, and applies the migrations to a Compose Postgres. Deploy to GKE reuses that workflow, then builds images such as the three-stage API Dockerfile, pushes them to Artifact Registry and renders the Kustomize overlay with images pinned to their digests. It runs the migrations before rolling out the services, so new code never runs against an old schema.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions reusable workflows (`on: workflow_call`) let a deploy pipeline run the same verification jobs as pull requests. Pinning Kubernetes images by digest instead of a tag ensures the exact image that was built is the one deployed.
